newsitem.title: USA: Record milk price but U.S. farm price index falls.
newsitem.headline: Record milk price but U.S. farm price index falls.

text.p: Milk prices hit a record high during September, thanks to strong demand and tight supplies, the Agriculture Department said Monday in its monthy farm price index report.

Despite the boost from dairy and higher cattle prices, the index fell 0.9 percent to 115 in September from 116 in August due to declines in hog and grain prices. The index is a guage of prices paid to farmers for their crops and livestock.
"The September all-milk price, at $16.20 (per 100 pounds), is a record high," the department said. "The previous high was $16 in December 1989."
Dairy prices have run at high levels for months. The department credited "tight supplies and good demand" for fuelling the record.
In early September, it said high milk prices were likely into 1997 because high feed prices would crimp output.
Although the overall index fell during August, it still was 10 points or 9.5 percent higher than one year ago. Higher prices for corn, milk, soybeans and cattle were responsible.
During September, soybeans sold for an average $7.85 a bushel, up 3 cents from August.

Corn prices fell 72 cents a bushel to average $3.58 but still were 89 cents higher than one year ago. Wheat sold for an average $4.19 a bushel, down 39 cents from August and 34 cents lower than one year ago. The new harvest, which replenished U.S. stockpiles, drove down prices.
Cotton sold for 70.9 cents a pound during September, 1 cent less than in August and 4.5 cents less than one year earlier.
Hogs averaged $54.40 per 100 pounds, down $5.30, due to a slowdown in exports and an increase in the number of hogs being sent to market.
Cattle prices surged $3.50 to average $63.80 per 100 pounds during September. Beef output is down in the face of high feed prices.
